---
title: "Changing Temporal Organisation of Heat Events Across India"
description: "Onset, duration, persistence, and recovery periods in hourly UTCI over 1980–2024."
status: "Thesis-derived manuscript in preparation"
year: 2026
---

## Research question

Is dangerous heat only becoming more intense, or is climate change also reorganising **when heat occurs, how long events persist, and how much recovery time separates them?**

## Approach

Using hourly UTCI over India from 1980–2024, the analysis tracks first and last annual exceedances, hot-season duration, heat-event frequency and length, nighttime exposure, and breaks between events.

At each native-resolution ERA5 grid point, hourly UTCI is converted into threshold-exceedance sequences. Metrics describing the temporal organisation of those sequences are calculated year by year, and long-run trends are tested using Mann-Kendall and autocorrelation-corrected Hamed-Rao Mann-Kendall tests.

## Selected results

### 1. Heat seasons can start earlier and end later

<figure class="research-figure">
<a href="/assets/figures/odf-slide-onset-end.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/odf-slide-onset-end.png" alt="Original thesis-defence slide showing trends in first and last annual UTCI threshold exceedances across India."></a>
<figcaption><strong>What to look for:</strong> the first-exceedance maps identify places where the heat season is moving earlier; the last-exceedance maps identify places where it is moving later. At the 38 °C threshold, the defence results show widespread earlier onset across North-East India, the coasts, the Indo-Gangetic Plain and other regions, alongside persistent later last exceedances.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 2. Events can persist longer while recovery breaks shrink

<figure class="research-figure">
<a href="/assets/figures/odf-slide-duration-breaks.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/odf-slide-duration-breaks.png" alt="Original thesis-defence slide showing trends in heat-event lengths and breaks between events across India."></a>
<figcaption><strong>What to look for:</strong> mean event lengths increase across large regions, while median event length is more stable in many places—consistent with a distribution increasingly shaped by long events. In North-East India both mean and median event length increase. Mean and median breaks between events shrink in North-East India and parts of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 3. Nighttime exposure is also changing

<figure class="research-figure">
<a href="/assets/figures/odf-slide-nighttime.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/odf-slide-nighttime.png" alt="Original thesis-defence slide showing trends in nighttime heat-stress exceedance across India."></a>
<figcaption><strong>What to look for:</strong> the nighttime heat-stress-exceedance fraction increases along both coasts in the defence results, raising the possibility of less physiological recovery overnight.</figcaption>
</figure>

Taken together, these results suggest that climate change is not only shifting the level of heat stress; it is also reorganising its **timing, persistence, clustering, and recovery structure**. The patterns are spatially heterogeneous, and the analysis is descriptive trend detection rather than causal attribution.

A related part of the thesis examines changing meteorological signatures of heat-stress exceedance using gridpoint-level logistic regression models.
